extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, authors, and academic publishers preparing manuscripts for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions for capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, numbers, abbreviations, and punctuation used in preparing academic manuscripts and publications (University of Chicago style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals and small capitals for date line, salutatory, signature, residence
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles should be set in capitals and small capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the date line to the right with one em’s indentation and preferably in smaller type than the body (example: CHICAGO, ILL., January 1, 1911). The salutation is set flush, followed by a colon, in the same type as the body and on a separate line unless run in with an address line. Example salutatory: My DEAR Mr. SMITH:. Signature and position lines: set and align per examples (e.g., CURTIS W. SCOTT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalized words in resolutions, notes, constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'WHEREAS'; in notes use 'Note.' followed by a period and a dash; in constitutions and by‑laws use 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example usages: Note.—It should be noticed that... . SECTION 1. This association shall be styled ... . Abbreviate 'section' after the first occurrence: Sec. 2. The object of the association...

rubrics_metrics.name: Small capitals for time-era abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M., and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals and without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C.; 1906 A.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-case for commonized derivatives of proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives (including verbs derived from proper names) should take lower-case initial letters when their origin is obscured by general usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china (leather), morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of italics for emphasis and foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or importance is to be lent and words/phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text that are not yet incorporated into English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of emphasis: 'This was, however, not the case.' Examples of foreign: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon’s coup d'état'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places normally printed in roman (e.g., Père Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau, the German Reichstag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize anglicized foreign words or certain foreign names
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize words of everyday occurrence that have become sufficiently anglicized or foreign titles/institution names whose English usage requires roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: café may be italicized when foreign, but many anglicized forms are set roman; do not italicize 'the German Reichstag' or 'Père Lagrange' when English usage favors roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize titles of publications (books, pamphlets, periodicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and single long poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals should be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night’s Dream; Paradise Lost; the Modern Language Review; the Chicago Tribune. Exception: may depart in lengthy bibliographies, tables, or where excessive italics would be visually distracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman type for books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of the Bible (canonical and apocryphal) and titles of ancient manuscripts and symbols used to designate manuscripts should be set in roman type, not italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: D16, M6, P, J. Also, books of the Bible printed roman (see rules for biblical abbreviations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize standard scholarly/legal reference words
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary and legal references, certain Latin and scholarly terms should be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.o., vide. (These are italicized in references and bibliographies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize certain common abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid italics for very common abbreviations used in scholarship and general writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. or vs. (versus), viz., etc. Also in indexes use 'See' and 'See also' roman for cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for direct quotations and special words
rubrics_metrics.description: Put direct cited prose passages and words/phrases requiring attention between quotation marks and set them in roman type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotation marks for citations run into text; for consecutive quotations from different authors when uninterrupted by original matter; for definitions of a word/phrase; for unusual, technical, or ironic words; and for translations where an English equivalent is presented. Example: Weltanschauung, 'world-view'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks for terms the writer highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the specific word or phrase to which attention is being directed in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the name 'Chicago'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-work titles in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of short poems, articles, lectures, papers, toasts, mottoes, and similarly short works should be set in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shelley’s 'To a Skylark'; article titles: 'Crusade' in Hastings’ Dictionary of the Bible. Note: some journals (e.g., Botanical Gazette) have alternative practices for footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set long quotations in smaller (reduced) type
rubrics_metrics.description: All prose extracts that will make five or more lines in the smaller type and all poetry citations of two lines or more ordinarily should be set in reduced type (smaller than main text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced citations generally should not have quotation marks (except in some noted cases), nor should quotation marks as a rule be used in connection with italics. Typical reductions: from 11-pt/10-pt to 9-pt; from 9-pt to 8-pt; from 8-pt to 6-pt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks must include ellipses and 'etc.' when needed for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when omission would not make clear that part of the original has been left out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Art. II, sec. 2, of the Constitution provides that 'each state shall appoint . . . .' '; place 'etc.' inside or outside quotes depending on whether it stands for omitted quoted matter or for matter outside the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat opening quotation marks at each paragraph of a broken quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation marks should indicate continuance across paragraphs; follow alignment conventions (cleared quotation marks projecting beyond alignment if desired).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations, single for nested
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; single quotation marks are used for quotations within quotations, alternating back and forth for additional levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example nested: 'The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out formal titles and honorifics before names; abbreviate Esq. after name
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address when they precede a name (exceptions listed). Abbreviate Esq. following a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out titles such as General, President, Sir, etc., except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon., St. (which are normally abbreviated). Do not set 'the Rev.' or 'the Hon.' except in quotations and correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out Christian (given) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full Christian names (e.g., George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviated forms in ordinary text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'Geo.' 'Chas.' 'Jno.' except in quoted matter or original signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number spelling conventions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out numbers of less than three digits except in statistical/technical contexts or long sequences; use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, enumerations, money, percentages, weights, and similar material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' but use figures for technical enumerations: 10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, $1,000, 9 per cent. If the largest number in a connected group contains three or more digits, use figures for all members of the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat connected numeric groups consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: When numbers occur in closely connected groups, treat them uniformly (either all spelled or all figures) based on the largest value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the largest contains three or more digits, use figures for all. Example: 'The force employed during the three months was 87, 93, and 106, respectively.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Round numbers (approximate) should be spelled
rubrics_metrics.description: Round or approximate numbers in ordinary prose are usually spelled out rather than given in figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but 'at 550' if specific). For special cases like '1,500' spelled out, write 'fifteen hundred' not 'one thousand five hundred'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers beginning a sentence are spelled out (or sentence reconstructed)
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, regardless of size, that begin a sentence should be spelled out; if impracticable, reconstruct the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example acceptable: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women... went down with the ship.' Or reconstruct: 'The total number of those who went down with the ship was 593 men...' (preferred if long numerals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sums of money in prose vs statistical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary prose, sums of money in isolated cases should be spelled out; in enumerations, statistical material, or many occurrences, use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example prose: 'The admission was two dollars.' Example statistical: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-of-day conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day is written in ordinary prose (e.g., 'at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon'); in statistical contexts and when using A.M./P.M., use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example statistical/time-of-day with figures: at 4:15 P.M. (omit 'o'clock' in such connections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages and centuries formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ages in ordinary prose are written out (e.g., 'eighty years and four months old'); centuries, dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, and political divisions are normally spelled out (nineteenth century, Fifth Dynasty, Fifty-fourth Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinal formatting may be used (Fifth Avenue). Use discretion when brevity is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out names of months in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months are spelled out in ordinary prose except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, nd, th), but use numerals in tables or statistical lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full 'United States' except specific contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'United States' in general text; use abbreviations like U.S. in certain contexts (e.g., General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S.S. 'Oregon'; in footnotes and similar references U.S. Geological Survey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment: 'United States' in prose, but abbreviations in certain formal/institutional references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for state names in lists/bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified two- or three-letter abbreviations for U.S. states, territories, and possessions following town names when in lists, bibliographical matter, etc.; omit the space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and full list provided (Cal., Ill., N.Y., Tex., Wyo., P.R. = Porto Rico, T.H. = Territory of Hawaii). Do not ordinarily use these abbreviations in running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abbreviations for 'Company', 'Brothers', and ampersand in technical/bibliographic matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) use abbreviations like Co., Bros., and ampersand (&) in commercial firm names; in ordinary text spell them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; in narrative text: 'Harper Brothers have recently published...' and 'American Steel and Wire Co.' spelled out when not proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'St.' for 'Saint' in place names; omit before apostles in usual usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' before place names and churches (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church). Preferably omit 'St.' in connection with apostles, evangelists, and church fathers in ordinary text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luke, Paul, Augustine (not 'St. Luke').

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviations for books and versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the prescribed abbreviations for books of the Bible (I and II Sam., Matt., John, etc.) and for commonly referred Bible versions (A.V., R.V., A.R.V., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive abbreviation lists provided for Old Testament, Apocrypha, New Testament, and versions (A.V.=Authorized Version, R.V.=Revised Version, A.R.V.=American Standard Revised Version, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate volume/number/chapter/section/page/figure in bibliographical references
rubrics_metrics.description: In footnotes and bibliographical matter, use standard abbreviations (Vol., No., Ps., Div., chap., art., sec., p., pp., col., vs., Fig., Figs.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I (Vols.), No. 1 (Nos.), pp. 5-7, pp. 5 f., pp. 5 sff.; use 'p.' for single page, 'pp.' for plural, 'Fig.' for figure, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric and measurement abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for weights, measures, and time when following numerals (e.g., m., mm., dm., cm., gm., gr., lb., oz., yd., ft., in., A for angstrom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (put period after some forms in certain journals); exceptions exist for some journals which use thin spaces and no period (Astrophysical Journal uses 12mm). See journal-specific notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite modern authors in office style; preserve original in Old English or essential cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In quotations from modern authors whose spelling/punctuation differ slightly from current usage, convert to office style; for Old English works or where fidelity is essential, follow the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should always be accurately quoted; use editorial discretion to modernize nonessential differences but retain originals where important to meaning or plan (see 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessive of proper names ending in sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form possessive of monosyllabic proper names ending in s or another sibilant by adding apostrophe + s; if the name has more than one syllable, form possessive by adding apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James’s Version, Burns’s poems, Marx’s theories; but: Moses' law, Jesus' birth. For proper names ending in a silent sibilant, add apostrophe + s regardless of syllables: Charlevoix’s discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite article 'a' vs 'an' usage before sounded h, long u, and 'one/once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a' before words beginning with sounded 'h', long 'u' (or 'ew'), and the words 'one'/'once'; use 'an' before vowel sounds otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic rendition, a union, a euphonious word; not 'an union'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ligatures (ae, oe) in modern English spellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligatures (æ, œ) in present-day English words adopted from Latin/Greek; write with 'ae', 'oe', or 'e' as appropriate; retain ligatures only in Old English and French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aesthetic (not æsthetic), Oedipus Tyrannus (Oedipus), but retain 'œuvre' in French. Also note variant forms like 'maneuver' vs 'manœuvre' preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Farther' should be used in the sense of spatial distance ('more remote', 'at a greater distance'); 'further' should be used in the sense of 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial forms retaining or omitting final -e
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' in the primary word (e.g., agreeing, hieing, singeing), while others omit the 'e' before the participial ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of retained e: dyeing, hoeing, shoeing. Examples of omitted e: abridging, changing, judging, acknowledging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the Manual’s preferred spellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the specific spellings recommended by the Manual for a large set of common words (detailed list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive spelled examples include abridgment, acknowledgment, aluminum, behavior, canceled, center, check, color, counselor, defense, fiber, flavor, harbor, judgment, maneuver, neighbor, mold, plow, program, rumor, theater, traveler, etc. Consult the list when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation marks should match the preceding character font
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'With the cry of Banzai,' the comma matches the preceding word's font; applies to punctuation adjacent to letters, numerals, or symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period usage: end of complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period indicates the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periods in conventional sentence-final positions; see additional rules for exceptions and placement with quotes/parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period after abbreviations with specified exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations except where mechanical or conventional exceptions apply (chemical symbols, 'per cent', some book formats, certain journal initials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas. Use caution with symbols (O, Fe), metric symbols may or may not take periods depending on journal practice. See noted exceptions for MS, linguistic epoch abbreviations (IE, OE, MHG) and certain journal initials (AJSL, ZAW).

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a period after Roman numerals even when they have the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running heads, centered headlines, side-heads, date lines, signatures, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period after running heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends that are not complete sentences, date lines at the top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are typographic headings or labels and do not receive terminal periods (see rules 279–283 for related terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the period inside the quotation marks. Place the period inside parentheses when the parenthetical matter is an independent sentence; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an absolute rule for periods with quotation marks: Tennyson’s 'In Memoriam.' For parentheses: if the parenthetical is part of the larger sentence, the period goes after the closing parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, emphatic, or ironical utterance and place it inside quotation marks or parentheses when it belongs to the quoted or parenthetical matter, otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' The placement follows whether the exclamation is part of the quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the question mark to mark a direct query or express doubt; place inside quotation marks or parentheses only when part of the quotation/parenthesis. Indirect questions should not be followed by a question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' Indirect: He asked whether he was ill. For combined contexts: The question: 'Who is who, and what is what?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon marks a greater discontinuity in grammatical construction than a semicolon and less than a period; used to (1) emphasize close connection between two clauses each a complete sentence, (2) separate a complete clause from an illustrative second clause, and (3) introduce formal statements, extracts, speeches in dialogue, lists, or amplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) 'This argument undeniably contains some force: Thus it is well known that...'; (2) 'Most countries have a national flower: France the lily, England the rose'; (3) 'We quote from the address: ...'. Do not use a colon when the following matter is immediately connected by a conjunction; before a clause in the middle of a sentence use a comma. Put a colon after salutatory phrases in letters: 'My DEAR Mr. Brown:' and as a separator between chapter:verse and hour:minute (see rule 134).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use centered colon between chapter:verse and hour:minute
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a centered colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:16; 4:15 P.M. (see respective time formatting rules).
